Fractal Space / Mathematical experiments
Copyright (c) 2026 Alex Vaos. MIT License; see LICENSE.txt.

These are new JavaScript/Canvas implementations of mathematical constructions.
The classic Klein bottle parametrization adapts a Three.js MIT example;
its attribution is below. No third-party artwork or shader code is included.
The directly served math-scenes.js and math.js are the complete source.
Regenerate the actual-renderer previews with node scripts/check-math.mjs --write.

Newton basins
-------------
Relaxed Newton iteration for f(z) = z^n - 1:
z_next = z - lambda f(z)/f'(z).
Default n=3, lambda=1. A residual squared below 1e-12 classifies a root;
55 iterations is the work limit. A zero/near-zero derivative or overflow
remains unclassified. Hue identifies the nearest root-of-unity angle only
after convergence. The raster has at most 440 samples across, so zooming
recomputes a finite approximation rather than revealing infinite precision.
Drag/arrow keys pan, scroll/pinch/+/- zoom, Space resets the view.

Hopf fibers
-----------
On S^3 in R^4, represented as C^2:
z1 = cos(eta) exp(it), z2 = sin(eta) exp(i(t+phi)).
The Hopf map is (2 Re(z1 conjugate(z2)), 2 Im(z1 conjugate(z2)),
|z1|^2-|z2|^2). It is constant in t for each fixed eta,phi.
Stereographic projection from w=1 sends (x,y,z,w) to (x,y,z)/(1-w).
The experiment draws three nearby eta values; each has equally spaced phi
values. Eta remains below pi/2 so the finite displayed fibers avoid the
projection pole. Each curve uses 96 segments. Distinct fibers link once;
a numerical Gauss-linking check verifies a representative pair.
Reference: Niles Johnson, A visualization of the Hopf fibration (2011),
https://nilesjohnson.net/hopf.html
Further mathematical reference: Zachary Treisman (2009),
https://nilesjohnson.net/hopf-articles/Treisman_Guide-to-Hopf-fibration.pdf
The references' images, animation, text and code are not included.

Torus knots and links
---------------------
R=1.6, r=.65. For d=gcd(p,q), draw d separate closed curves:
theta=(p/d)t; phi=(q/d)t + 2*pi*k/p, k=0,...,d-1.
Position = ((R+r cos(phi)) cos(theta),
            (R+r cos(phi)) sin(theta), r sin(phi)).
Each component uses 720 segments. d=1 gives a knot; d>1 gives a link.
Space advances p. The equation shown on the page describes the coprime
case; the explanation describes reduction and phase offsets for links.
Curves are projected and segments depth-sorted, with screen-space strand
width. They are not physical elastic tubes. Default (3,2) is a trefoil.

Gyroid field
------------
g(x,y,z)=sin(x)cos(y)+sin(y)cos(z)+sin(z)cos(x).
Draw g=c over one or two periods per axis. This trigonometric level set
is a nodal approximation to a gyroid, not an exact minimal surface.
A 14-cell grid per period is split into six tetrahedra per cube, with
linear edge interpolation. The mesh therefore approximates the level set.
Its analytic gradient gives lighting; triangle depth sorting gives occlusion.
The bounded domain is intentionally open at its faces, without invented caps.
Background reference: Alan H. Schoen (1970), Infinite periodic minimal
surfaces without self-intersections, NASA TN D-5541:
https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/19700020472
That report is background on minimal surfaces; the displayed nodal equation
and this finite mesh should not be mistaken for an exact representation.

Reaction-diffusion
------------------
Gray-Scott fixed-step Euler simulation on a periodic 144x96 grid:
A_next=A+lap(A)-A*B^2+f*(1-A)
B_next=B+.5*lap(B)+A*B^2-(k+f)*B
The nine-point Laplacian has weights -1 at center, .2 at axial neighbors,
.05 at diagonal neighbors. dt=1. Concentrations are clamped to [0,1].
Both fields update simultaneously via separate next-state buffers.
Initial A=1,B=0; eighteen seeded patches add B. The player warms up 600
steps, then advances six simulation steps per 30Hz tick. Pausing stops
evolution; painting B changes the current state without advancing time.
Changing rates preserves the state; selecting a preset or a new variation
reinitializes it. Uniform A=1,B=0 is a fixed point; periodic pure diffusion
conserves concentration. Tests compare all boundary stencil values with
an independent modular-coordinate reference implementation.
Brush: drag to seed B; arrow keys move, Enter plants. Space cycles regimes.
Reference for the model and stencil: Karl Sims, Reaction-Diffusion Tutorial,
https://www.karlsims.com/rd.html
No reference images or implementation code are copied.

Clifford attractor
------------------
x_next=sin(a*y)+c*cos(a*x)
y_next=sin(b*x)+d*cos(b*y)
Both use the old x,y simultaneously. Default a=-1.4,b=1.6,c=1,d=.7.
The initial 100 iterates are discarded. Accumulate a 256x256 visit histogram,
starting with 80,000 visits. Each tick adds 5,000 until the cap of 1,500,000.
Logarithmic density, normalized to the current maximum and raised to
the power .55 to lift faint structure, controls color.
The domain bound is derived from |x|<=1+|c|, |y|<=1+|d|.
Changing a or b restarts the histogram; Space selects a,b,c,d presets.
Depending on parameters the map may have a strange attractor, a periodic
orbit, or a fixed point. The player does not claim all parameters are chaotic.

Shared interface
----------------
Drag/arrow orbit, scroll/pinch zoom for 3-D constructions. Plane navigation
and simulation/attractor controls are specific to their respective models.
The system/light/dark site theme covers all UI, equations, and help. Artwork
colors stay independent. Reduced-motion users receive a paused initial state,
including precomputed simulation/attractor snapshots; manual controls work.
PNG save captures the actual canvas. No external rendering dependency is used.


Klein bottle and torus (2026-10-28)
----------------------------------
The Klein bottle uses the classic piecewise bottle immersion from Three.js
ParametricFunctions.klein, algebraically reorganized, scaled and reoriented
here. Copyright three.js authors, MIT. Full original notice is distributed
in math/threejs-LICENSE.txt. Reference inspected 2026-10-28:
https://github.com/mrdoob/three.js/blob/dev/examples/jsm/geometries/ParametricFunctions.js
Only the small parametrization is adapted; no Three.js library is needed.
Our mesh generation, controls, lighting, and rendering are new.

Before display scaling, with t=neck width, r=t*(2-cos u):
x=3 cos(u)(1+sin(u)) + r cos(u)cos(v), for 0<=u<pi;
x=3 cos(u)(1+sin(u)) + r cos(v+pi), for pi<=u<=2pi.
z=-8 sin(u) - r sin(u)cos(v), for 0<=u<pi;
z=-8 sin(u), for pi<=u<=2pi.
y=-r sin(v).
The 3-D image self-intersects: crossing sheets do not join in the abstract
surface. Boundary identifications are (0,v)~(2pi,pi-v) and (u,0)~(u,2pi).
This reversal is what distinguishes the Klein bottle from the torus.
Its non-orientability prevents a consistent global normal; shading is local
and double-sided. This piecewise bottle shape is a visualization of the
abstract surface, not a smooth isometric embedding. Surface reveal below
one opens the parameter sheet into a cutaway; it is then no longer closed.
Background: Thomas F. Banchoff / Surfaces Beyond the Third Dimension,
https://www.math.union.edu/~dpvc/TFB/Art/PAC-9603/tour/klein/klein.html
No images or animations from that exhibition are copied.

Torus: ((R+r cos v)cos u, r sin v, (R+r cos v)sin u),
u,v in [0,2pi]. R ranges 1.2..2.4; r ranges .2..1.1, so R>r always.
The hole radius is R-r. Both parameter directions are identified without
reversal. This is an orientable ring torus; horn and spindle cases are
intentionally outside the controls' range.

Each full surface has 72x36 vertices and 5,184 triangles. Seam vertices are
identified by their parameter-space gluing, not by spatial coincidence.
Tests check every edge has two incident faces and V-E+F=0, and traverse the
face adjacency to verify orientability for the torus and its obstruction
for the Klein bottle. Cutaways have boundary edges and are labeled open.

Display: depth-sorted Canvas triangles, local lighting, and a parameter grid.
Space cycles surface styles: Klein starts in glass, torus in solid. Glass
uses translucent painter's-algorithm triangles and is an illustrative view,
not an exact order-independent transparency solution at intersecting sheets.
Parameters, manual rotation, and view switching work while paused.


Möbius strip and Schwarz lantern (2026-10-29)
-------------------------------------------
Both are original MIT-licensed implementations of standard mathematical
constructions. No source code or images from a reference are copied.

Möbius strip: R=1.7, u in [0,2pi], v in [-width,width]:
f(u,v)=((R+v cos(hu/2))cos u, v sin(hu/2),
        (R+v cos(hu/2))sin u).
The half-turn count h is odd (1,3,5), so f(2pi,v)=f(0,-v).
The 96x16-cell mesh identifies that reversed seam. It has Euler
characteristic zero, is non-orientable, and has exactly one boundary loop.
The boundary tracer follows f(t,width), t=0..4pi. It visits the opposite
parameter edge after 2pi and returns after 4pi. The marker is drawn visibly
over the surface to make its journey easy to follow. The light/shading is
local and two-sided. This is a geometric ribbon, not a material bending model.
Slider steps are aligned to their minimum so 1,3,5 stay odd in the UI.

Schwarz lantern: radius r=1.5, height H=3. Use n evenly spaced vertices on
each of m+1 polygon rings. Every odd ring is shifted by pi/n; adjacent
rings are joined with 2n congruent isosceles triangles per band.
There are 2mn faces; no end caps are included. The mesh is an orientable
annulus with two boundary loops. Every vertex lies on the cylinder.
One triangle has area r*sin(pi/n)*sqrt((H/m)^2+r^2*(1-cos(pi/n))^2), hence
A=2mn*r*sin(pi/n)*sqrt((H/m)^2+r^2*(1-cos(pi/n))^2).
The readout compares A with the cylinder lateral area 2pi*r*H. It also
sums the geometry independently in tests using cross products.

For simultaneous n,m -> infinity, the area converges to the cylinder's
area exactly when m/n^2 -> 0. A sequence m=n works; m=n^2 has a larger
finite limiting ratio; m=n^3 diverges. The analytic tests cover these
sequences without constructing unbounded meshes. The interactive mesh is
bounded by n<=40,m<=160, at most 12,800 triangles. This numerical-control
limit does not claim to realize an infinite sequence on screen.

Construction reference: John M. Sullivan / Matteo Petrera, Geometry II,
TU Berlin, exercise sheet 1 (2010), Exercise 2, The Schwarz lantern:
https://page.math.tu-berlin.de/~sullivan/L/10S/Geo2/ex1.pdf
Its notation swaps the names of the two counts compared with this player;
our n always means vertices around each ring, m always means bands.


Gyroid views (2026-10-29)
------------------------
Gyroid (existing route gyroid-field) now cycles solid, wireframe and glass
with Space or the surface button. All three use the same sampled level set;
view changes preserve both c and the repeat count. Wireframe shows the
actual triangle mesh; glass uses translucent depth-sorted triangles to
expose the repeated passages. This is illustrative transparency, not
order-independent transparency at every overlap. The level-set equation
remains a nodal approximation rather than the exact minimal gyroid.
Controls, pause, reduced motion and PNG export apply to every view.


Sierpiński triangle (2026-10-29)
------------------------------
Original MIT-licensed midpoint-subdivision implementation, with no external
code or assets. Begin with an equilateral triangle of side 2 and area sqrt(3).
Join edge midpoints, remove the central triangle, and recurse on the three
survivors. At depth n there are 3^n retained triangles, each scaled by 2^-n,
and total remaining area (3/4)^n times the starting area. The infinite limit
has Hausdorff dimension log(3)/log(2). Finite images are approximations, not
a claim that a filled finite-depth triangle mesh has non-integer dimension.

Depth is capped at 8 (6,561 leaves and 3,280 central holes). Construction
progress p sets phase n*p. Completed generations remove their full holes;
the next generation's holes scale about their centroids by the fractional
phase f. During that interpolation the remaining area fraction is
(3/4)^floor(n*p) * (1 - f^2/4), with no extra cut at the completed target.
Space advances to an exact integer generation; it wraps to the filled
initial triangle after the target. Depth zero avoids any division by zero.

The 2-D view uses the shared complex-plane pan/zoom controller with its own
vertical center. Zoom is anchored under the cursor; progress and colors do
not rebuild the deterministic recursion model. Tests verify leaf counts,
area conservation, shrink factors, intermediate areas and construction
steps, including reduced motion and zero/maximum depth.


Koch snowflake (2026-10-29)
--------------------------
Original MIT-licensed implementation of the standard construction; no external
source code or images. Begin with a counterclockwise equilateral triangle of
side 2, perimeter P0=6 and area A0=sqrt(3). Trisect each edge and replace its
middle third with an outward equilateral peak. Every edge becomes four edges.
At generation n: N=3*4^n, edge length=2/3^n, P/P0=(4/3)^n,
A/A0=8/5-(3/5)*(4/9)^n. The limiting perimeter is infinite; limiting area
is 8*A0/5. The limiting boundary dimension is log(4)/log(3), not the dimension
of a finite polygon. Depth is capped at 7 (49,152 edges).

Progress p sets phase n*p. Completed generations use the exact polygon;
the next generation raises each peak to fraction f of its final height.
The area ratio during this step adds f/3*(4/9)^generation. The perimeter
ratio is (4/3)^generation*(2+sqrt(1+3*f*f))/3. It is not linear in f.
Space advances an exact generation and wraps back to the starting triangle.
Depth zero is valid. Geometry is cached across progress, pan and color changes.
Checks independently sum edge lengths and signed shoelace area, including
partial generations, and exercise the controller with reduced motion.


Double pendulum (2026-10-29)
----------------------------
Original MIT implementation of the ideal equal-mass, equal-length double
pendulum: two point masses m=1 kg, rigid massless rods L=1 m, g=9.81 m/s^2.
No friction, driving force, collision handling or small-angle approximation.
Angles a,b are from the downward vertical. With u=da/dt,v=db/dt,d=a-b:
2*a''+cos(d)*b''=-2*g*sin(a)-sin(d)*v^2;
cos(d)*a''+b''=-g*sin(b)+sin(d)*u^2.
Solve this 2x2 linear system (determinant 2-cos(d)^2 >= 1) for acceleration.
E=u^2+v^2/2+u*v*cos(d)-g*(2*cos(a)+cos(b)).
The displayed drift is abs(E-E0)/(3mgL), in parts per million, not relative
to E0 (which can be zero). The amber twin adds 0.01 degrees to initial b.
It illustrates sensitivity for chaotic releases, not a Lyapunov estimate.
Low-energy starting positions may remain regular.

Each 1/30-second simulation tick takes eight fourth-order Runge-Kutta
substeps of 1/240 second. Rendering never advances physics. The retained
trail has at most 901 samples spanning 30 seconds. A slow display slows
simulation time rather than taking unstable long integration steps.
Pause, reduced motion, hidden-tab suspension and modal Help stop stepping.
Reset repeats the same deterministic release from rest; changing a starting
angle also resets both trajectories and trails without resuming a pause.
Reference for the standard equations: Erik Neumann, myPhysicsLab,
https://www.myphysicslab.com/pendulum/double-pendulum-en.html
No source code, prose, or visual assets from the reference are copied.
Tests check coupled-equation residuals, rod lengths, symmetry, rest states,
time reversal, fourth-order convergence, bounded trails, energy drift and
repeatability, as well as actual pointer/keyboard/paused player behavior.


Gravity, waves, and attracting fields (2026-10-29)
-------------------------------------------------
All four additions are original MIT implementations with no copied source,
prose or visual assets. Equations use normalized units.

Orbital gravity: a(r)=-mu*r/|r|^3, mu=GM in [.25,2.5]. The star is fixed;
planets follow its attraction independently. Six initial radii are
.8,1.15,1.6,2.15,2.8,3.55; initial tangential speed is k/sqrt(r), k=.2..2.2.
Circular motion requires k=sqrt(mu), escape k>=sqrt(2mu). Changing gravity
holds the requested launch k fixed and resets the six planets.
E=|v|^2/2-mu/r; h=x*vy-y*vx; e=sqrt(1+2Eh^2/mu^2).
Velocity-Verlet uses twelve steps of 1/360 per simulation tick of 1/30:
r'=r+v*dt+a(r)*dt^2/2; v'=v+(a(r)+a(r'))*dt/2.
Swept segment intersection detects impact at star radius .18 before the
new acceleration is evaluated. An impact absorbs the planet. Unbound,
outward-moving planets beyond radius 200 retire. Body count is capped at
12; each trail retains 901 samples (30 time units). Launch positions must
have radius .35..8; drag velocity=.8*(end-start), capped at magnitude 8.
Space restores six planets; canceled pointers and Help discard launches.
Physics: https://science.nasa.gov/learn/basics-of-space-flight/chapter3-3/
Numerics: https://users.utu.fi/tejohy/teaching/simu/L42.html

Interference pool: u=.32*sum(cos(2*pi*r_i/lambda-omega*t+phi_i)
/sqrt(1+.8*r_i)), omega=2*pi*.6, sources at (+/-separation/2,0).
The radial attenuation is illustrative. This is prescribed coherent wave
superposition, not a fluid simulation or boundary-value solver. Opposite
phase cancels exactly at x=0; matching phase reinforces there. A 36x36-cell
wire surface samples the analytic formula. Animation uses simulation time;
P and reduced motion freeze both waves and automatic view rotation.

Rössler: x'=-y-z, y'=x+a*y, z'=.2+z*(x-c). RK4 dt=.025,
1,000 transient steps followed by 8,000 retained samples. Every computed
point must be finite with absolute coordinates below 100; leaving this
window stops the trace and displays a label. Parameters can yield regular
or chaotic motion. The view rotates around a finite sampled curve.
Reference: O. E. Rössler, An equation for continuous chaos (1976),
https://doi.org/10.1016/0375-9601(76)90101-8

Magnetic pendulums: three poles on a unit equilateral ring, height h=.35;
V=.15*|r|^2-sum(q/sqrt(|m_i-r|^2+h^2)); r''=-grad(V)-gamma*r'.
This is a simplified smooth potential for planar bobs. The exact energy
rate is dE/dt=-gamma*|v|^2. RK4 uses eight steps of 1/240 per 1/30 tick.
Twenty-one releases start from rest on radius 2.25; dragging releases a
small group near the cursor. Each trail retains 361 samples (12 time units).
Speed below .015 and force below .02 for 60 ticks retires a bob as settled.
This finite stopping tolerance is an illustrative equilibrium criterion.
Color identifies the nearest well; it is not an exact basin classification.


Orbit ink (2026-10-29)
---------------------
Original MIT implementation of an orthographic 3-D drawing surface.
Camera rotation R=Rx(pitch)*Ry(yaw+turn). A pointer sample at (px,py) maps to
camera coordinates ((px-cx)/scale,(cy-py)/scale,penDepth), then to world
coordinates with R inverse. The stored world point never changes when the
camera or rotation speed changes. Projecting it immediately returns the
original pixel coordinates and chosen camera depth. Every visible sample
uses this same transform, including when drawing while paused.

The automatic turn accumulates speed*dt, dt=1/30, in radians. Its phase is
wrapped to one revolution. Speed changes do not jump to a new orientation.
While a pointer is held, simulation ticks also sample its last screen
position, allowing a stationary pen to trace a curve through rotating space.
Pointer movement samples immediately. Nearby points less than .003 world
units apart are skipped. Existing strokes retain their starting ink color.

The view starts with an empty drawing and a rotating reference cage/grid.
A thumbnail example is generated by simulated input through the same scene
API; the browser never preloads it into the user's drawing. Up to 12,000
points and 128 strokes are retained. One cleared drawing can be restored
with Undo; repeated clears replace that snapshot, bounding memory. Undo
removes the latest stroke, then restores a prior clear if no strokes remain.
Rendering projects the strokes in chunks of at most 17 points, sorting them
by average depth; glow is illustrative rather than exact solid occlusion.

One pointer draws; adding a second ends the stroke and switches to pinch
zoom. Pointer up/cancel, blur, hidden tabs and Help finish strokes so the
next gesture cannot join unrelated points. Automatic rotation pauses under
P, Help, visibility suspension and reduced-motion defaults; manual drawing,
depth changes, undo and orbit remain available. R resets the view without
erasing geometry. The Clear button is undoable. PNG saves the current view.


Fibonacci sculpture (2026-10-29)
------------------------------
Original MIT implementation. F1=F2=1, Fn=Fn-1+Fn-2 for n>=3; the view uses
1..12 terms, ending at F12=144. The ratio Fn/Fn-1 tends to phi=(1+sqrt(5))/2.
At one term the ratio is absent because F0=0. The readout shows the current
ratio, phi, and their absolute difference without implying a finite ratio
is exactly phi.

Place the first unit square at (0,0), then attach each new square around
the existing rectangle in directions right, up, left, down. Each new side
is the next Fibonacci number. Footprints are interior-disjoint and fill the
rectangle: sum(Fi^2)=Fn*Fn+1. At full extrusion all three cube edge lengths
are Fi, so volume is Fi^3. Fractional extrusion gives height Fi*extrusion;
zero extrusion renders the square tiling as a double-sided planar surface.

Each square contains a quarter circle of radius Fi. Arc center corners
cycle top-right, top-left, bottom-left, bottom-right. The starting angle is
pi+i*pi/2, traversed counterclockwise through pi/2. Adjacent arc endpoints
coincide in the footprint. The 3-D path runs at each cube's height with
vertical connectors between arcs. These quarter circles form a Fibonacci
spiral approximation associated with the exact logarithmic golden spiral.
The lifted path and extrusion are this artwork's spatial interpretation.

The orthographic camera normalizes by the bounding-box half-diagonal,
keeping each displayed construction within a sphere of radius 2.4. Changing
term count refits the view; all relative lengths stay exact. Translucent
faces are depth sorted; the spiral and numeric labels overlay the geometry
for readability. Labels below 17 pixels or overlapping a larger term are omitted;
the full sequence remains in the status readout. Space adds a term, wrapping
from twelve back to one. Camera, color and extrusion changes preserve the
cached footprint geometry. Pause and reduced motion stop automatic rotation
while every manual control and PNG export stays available.

Mathematical reference: Eric W. Weisstein, Fibonacci Number, MathWorld:
https://mathworld.wolfram.com/FibonacciNumber.html
Golden spiral reference: https://mathworld.wolfram.com/GoldenSpiral.html
No source code, prose, or images from these references are copied.


Mountain terrain
----------------
Original MIT-licensed implementation in mountain-terrain.js. A 32-bit integer
lattice hash feeds bounded 2-D value noise with quintic interpolation
6t^5−15t^4+10t^3. Two coarse noise fields warp the sampling domain. Five
rotated noise octaves contribute squared ridges (1−abs(N))^2, with
lacunarity 1.9 and persistence 0.25 + 0.43 × roughness. A coarse component
adds broader landforms. The finite grid is normalized once to [−1,1].

Positive samples become H × f^1.55, negative samples become
−V × (−f)^0.9. Thus the field's highest and lowest sampled points reach
the chosen mountain height H and negative valley depth −V exactly, in
relative units. Height/depth edits preserve the seed and normalized field;
roughness rebuilds the noise with that same seed. Landscape depth scales
z coordinates only, preserving every elevation. A 64×64 grid produces
8,192 consistently oriented surface triangles. Vertical side walls and a
bottom close the cut section at y=−V−0.22.

Perspective projection uses a camera distance larger than the bounding
sphere, so the denominator stays positive for all orbit angles. Faces are
backface-culled and depth sorted; this Canvas painter approximates visibility
for highly overlapping projected triangles. Color and directional lighting
show height and slope. Contours interpolate twelve height levels on the
triangulation. Wireframe preserves solid depth occlusion. No erosion,
hydrology, physical units, or real-world elevation data are simulated.

New terrain changes only the seed. Surface, Contours, and Wireframe share
the same geometry. Animation rotates the camera rather than morphing the
landscape. Pause/reduced motion preserve manual edits, orbit and PNG capture.


Ripple plane
------------
Original MIT-licensed damped-wave solver and 3D renderer in ripple-plane.js.
A 64×64-cell grid spans 6.4 relative units per side. The finite-difference
recurrence approximates u_tt + gamma*u_t = c²*(u_xx+u_zz), with centered
spatial differences and damping centered in time. Four 1/120 substeps give
each 1/30 display tick. At maximum speed 2.4, the Courant number is 0.20
on this grid, below 1/sqrt(2); even the helper's maximum grid has CFL 0.30.
The outer ring is fixed and an eight-cell damping strip softens reflections.
It is an approximate absorbing edge, not a perfectly matched boundary.

A droplet adds a compact, Gaussian-derived displacement to both current
and previous buffers, preserving instantaneous velocity. Its profile is
−A*(1−q/2)*exp(−q/2), q=r²/sigma², truncated at four sigma. Multiple
impulses superpose in the same linear field. The truncated/discretized
profile only approximately has zero net displacement; it does not model
water volume or a falling object's dynamics. Speed/damping changes retain
the field history; droplet size affects future drops only. Render height
is H*tanh(u), a bounded visual scale for dense overlapping impulses. The
physics itself remains linear; there is no nonlinear fluid solver.

The height field is triangulated and shaded with a perspective camera.
Clicks/taps use the nearest ray/triangle hit on its actual displaced
triangles. Hover uses the rest plane as a light-weight target estimate.
Drag, cancel, pinch, blur and help actions suppress accidental droplets.
The camera stays still while waves move; drag/Shift+arrows orbit it.
Pause/reduced motion freeze propagation and preserve all manual controls.
Two finite initialized ripples demonstrate the surface even when paused.
R/Clear water removes every wave while retaining parameters and camera.
Impact indicators retain at most 32 entries and disappear after one second;
the full field retains their waves. At negligible displacement the solver
rests. Surface lighting, faint grid, and impact rings are illustrative;
there are no textures, copied source code, or external fluid dependencies.

Extended controls (2026-10-29): torus radii include self-intersecting spindle
surfaces and the horn limit; Möbius half-turns remain odd (1–15). Finite
construction depths are 9 for Sierpiński triangles and 8 for Koch snowflakes.
Fibonacci tilings support 20 terms; extrusion above 1 stretches cube heights.
Terrain roughness reaches 2 with five finite octaves, normalized as before.
Ripple speed 0–5 has a maximum Courant number of 0.625 on the finest grid,
below the two-dimensional five-point stencil limit 1/sqrt(2).

Ball drop (original MIT implementation): constant uniform gravity; no air drag
or spin. Exact flight segments are joined at analytically computed floor
collisions. Coefficient of restitution e rescales impact velocity; vertical
energy and peak heights retain e^2 after each bounce. An outgoing velocity
below 0.015 m/s is resolved as rest to end the inelastic collision accumulation.
Earth 9.81, Moon 1.62, Mars 3.71, Jupiter 24.79 m/s^2 are approximate preset
values; Jupiter uses equatorial reference gravity, not a solid surface.
Planetary reference: https://ssd.jpl.nasa.gov/planets/phys_par.html

Liquid cursor (original MIT implementation): scalar fields r^4/(d^2+0.02r^2)^2
are summed, with the visible boundary at cohesion times the sum = 1. The
cursor has the same field as every droplet. Analytic derivatives shade the
height z = 0.6 sqrt(1-1/F) in the visible region. The shader-like Canvas
raster has a maximum long edge of 400 samples. Damped center motion and
local cursor attraction are artistic heuristics, not a volume-conserving
fluid simulation. A maximum of 32 floating drops bounds work.

Spectrum analyzer (original MIT): browser AnalyserNode float frequency data,
FFT sizes 1024–16384, bin spacing sampleRate/FFTsize; peak estimation uses
three-bin parabolic interpolation in dB. Log bands cover 20 Hz–min(20 kHz,
Nyquist), excluding DC, and display each band's maximum bin. RMS level is
20 log10(RMS amplitude) dBFS with a display floor at -120 dBFS, not SPL.
Spectral magnitudes depend on the browser's Blackman window and smoothing.
A 64-frame waterfall and 96 frequency bands bound rendering work.
Reference: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/AnalyserNode
Reference: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/MediaDevices/getUserMedia

Orbit Breach (original MIT): regular polygon wall quads and a circular player
hitbox at fixed radius. Collision checks convex containment and edge distance
against the rendered coordinates. A fixed 240 Hz model uses bounded substeps
(maximum 0.25 seconds per advance call); display deltas are capped at 0.05 s.
At most 12 rings are retained. Seeded gap walks shift by at most two sectors;
100-second simulated runs exercise reachability across all 9 arena/mode pairs.
Reference inspiration: https://superhexagon.com/
